title: The witness who never sleeps
hookLine: the Katha Upanishad speaks of one who stays awake in those who sleep
carry: sakshi: the witness awake in those who sleep

lines: A QUIET WARD AT THREE A.M.
ONE IS AWAKE, WAKING NO ONE.
cards: A night nurse walks a quiet ward at three in the morning. Every bed holds a sleeper. Some breathe slowly.
One talks in a dream. One turns over and pulls the blanket up. The nurse is the only one awake, moving from bed to bed, seeing it all, waking no one.
The Katha Upanishad has a line that sounds like that ward, but it's describing something inside each sleeper. It says someone stays awake in us while we sleep.

teach.h: NACHIKETAS WAITS THREE NIGHTS AT DEATH'S DOOR.
teach.b: The Katha Upanishad is Death's teaching to a boy named Nachiketas, who went to Death's house and waited three nights without food until Death came home and, as a host who had kept a guest waiting, owed him three wishes.
His last wish was to know what lies beyond death. In the fifth section of Death's answer comes this, in paraphrase.

The Person who is awake in those who sleep, shaping one desire after another, that is the bright one, that is Brahman, that alone is called the deathless. Even while we dream, something is awake and doing the shaping.

teach.h: THE ATMAN: THE ONE WHO SEES.
teach.b: Hindus call it the atman, the Self: not the body, not the thoughts, but the one who sees them. The Gita turns the image around.

What is night for all beings, Krishna says in chapter two, in that the self-mastered one is awake. The world's busy daytime is a kind of sleep, and what the world sleeps through, the sage is awake to.
Another Upanishad gives this watcher a name: sakshi, the witness. The Shvetashvatara calls the one God, hidden in all beings, the witness, the one who knows, alone, beyond the qualities.
That's where the yoga nidra days have been heading: the Goddess holding Vishnu's sleep, the Mandukya's fourth, the resolve, the senses gathered in.
Read side by side, each can be taken as pointing toward one thing: rest so deep it looks like sleep, with the witness still awake.
Teachers of the practice say it plainly: the body sleeps, and awareness doesn't.

how: Hindus who study Vedanta speak of the sakshi, the witness that remains through waking, dream and deep sleep; teachers of yoga nidra describe the practice as deep rest for the body with awareness kept awake.

o: staying up all night to keep watch in prayer
sleepwalking while some part of you dreams on
deep rest for the body, with the witness awake

p: night for all beings; the sage is awake
God hidden in all beings, the witness

s: the Katha Upanishad says nothing in a person is awake during sleep
it speaks of the Person who is awake in those who sleep, shaping desire after desire.
in the Gita, what is night for all beings is where the self-mastered one is awake
Krishna says it in chapter two, and turns it around: where beings are awake is night for the sage.
sakshi means the one who acts
sakshi is the witness, the one who sees.

games.q: you're lying deep in rest, the body heavy. a thought drifts past. what do you do?
o: chase it, to see where it goes.
push it away to get back to rest.
notice it, as the one who sees.
games.why: the texts set the witness at the center: the one who sees the thought, the breath and the heavy body, and wakes none of them.

practice: Lie down or sit back, eyes closed, and let the body go heavy, one part at a time, while the breath does what it does. Then notice that something is noticing all this: the heaviness, the breath, a sound in the room, a stray thought.
Don't try to find the noticer or picture it; just rest as the one who sees, like the nurse on the ward, waking no one.

wordCard.voice: Yoga nidra. The sleep of yoga. Deep rest for the body, with the witness, the sakshi, still awake.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: sakshi, witness. The one who sees, awake through waking, dream and sleep.

carryVoice: Your line: sakshi, the witness awake in those who sleep. Tomorrow, the eyes open, on a single flame. Sleep well tonight.
